name: Zephaniah
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text). It was checked against the Hebrew Minor Prophets scrolls from Qumran (4QXII, 4QXII-b, -c, and -g) and Wadi Murabba‘at (MurXII, early 2nd century AD), whose text is very close to the Masoretic Text. The transcriptions used are Martin Abegg’s, as published in the ETCBC Dead Sea Scrolls dataset. It was also checked against the Septuagint, using Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Portions of Zephaniah also survive in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr, about the turn of the era), which is a revision of the Septuagint toward the Hebrew. Its readings could not be checked directly, so any that are cited are marked “reported.” Significant differences are footnoted; differences of spelling and damage to the scrolls are not. The divine title YHWH Tseva’ot is translated “Yahweh of Armies” (see the note at 2:9). Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible: in Zephaniah, English and Hebrew verse numbers are the same.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Zephaniah the son of Cushi, the son of Gedaliah, the son of Amariah, the son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah.{a}

“I will utterly sweep away everything
from upon the face of the ground,” declares Yahweh.

“I will remove people and livestock;
I will remove the birds that fly in the sky
and the fish of the ocean,
and the idols{b} along with the wicked.
I will eliminate humanity
from the face of the earth,” declares Yahweh.

those who have turned back from following Yahweh,
who have not sought Yahweh nor inquired of him.”

Hush in the presence of the Lord Yahweh!
The day of Yahweh is close;
Yahweh has made ready a slaughter
and set apart those he has invited.

“And it shall come to pass on the day of Yahweh’s sacrifice
that I will punish the princes and the sons of the king,
and all who are clothed in foreign clothing.

On that day I will punish
all who leap across the threshold,{e}
and those who load their lords’ houses
with violent loot and lies.

“On that day,” declares Yahweh,
“there shall be the sound of a cry from the Fish Gate,
a wail from the Second Quarter,{f}
and a great crash from the hills.

At that time I will search Jerusalem with lamps,
and I will punish the men
who are thickening on their dregs,{h}
who say in their heart,
‘Yahweh will not do good,
nor will he do evil.’

Their wealth shall become plunder
and their houses a waste.
Though they build houses, they shall not dwell in them;
though they plant vineyards, they shall not drink their wine.”

The great day of Yahweh is near,
it is near and hurries greatly.
Hark, the day of Yahweh! It is bitter;
the mighty man cries aloud there.

That day will be a day of rage,{i}
a time of anguish and misery,
a time of wreckage and waste,
a time of darkness and dimness,
a time of storm clouds and blackness,

a day of the ram’s horn and of the war cry
against the walled cities
and against the high corner towers.

“I will bring distress upon mankind,
and they shall walk like the blind,
because they have sinned against Yahweh;
their blood shall be poured out like dust,
and their flesh like dung.”

Neither their silver nor their gold
will have power to save them
on the day of Yahweh’s fury.
His blazing jealousy will consume
the whole earth,
for he will bring a sudden, terrifying end
to everyone living on the planet.

notes.text: Zephaniah means “Yahweh has hidden” or “Yahweh has treasured up”; Cushi means “Cushite”; Gedaliah, “Yahweh is great”; Amariah, “Yahweh has spoken”; and Hezekiah, “Yahweh strengthens.” This Hezekiah may be the king of that name (reigned about 715–686 BC), though the text does not say so. Josiah reigned about 640–609 BC.
The Hebrew phrase “and the stumbling blocks” (perhaps meaning idols) is obscure, and the Septuagint lacks it.
Hebrew kemarim, a word used for priests of foreign gods (compare 2 Kings 23:5 and Hosea 10:5). The Septuagint has “the names of the priests.”
Malcam means “their king.” It probably refers to Milcom, the god of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:5), and some ancient versions read “Milcom.” The Septuagint has “their king.”
This may refer to a pagan custom (compare 1 Samuel 5:5), or to palace servants rushing in to seize the goods of others.
The Fish Gate and the Second Quarter (Hebrew Mishneh) were in the northern part of Jerusalem.
Hebrew Makhtesh, “mortar” or “hollow,” probably a district of Jerusalem. “The people of Canaan” may also be translated “the merchants.”
That is, like wine left too long on its sediment: complacent and stagnant (compare Jeremiah 48:11).
In the Latin Vulgate, the opening words of this verse are Dies irae, dies illa (“A day of wrath, that day”). They gave the medieval hymn Dies irae its name.

verses.text:
Gather yourselves together and gather,{a}
O nation without shame,

before the decree brings forth—
like chaff the day passes by—
before the fierce anger of Yahweh
comes upon you,
before there comes upon you
the day of the anger of Yahweh.

Disaster for those living along the coast,
you nation of Cretans!{d}
Yahweh’s message is aimed at you,
Canaan, land of the Philistines:
I will wipe you out, leaving no one living there.

And the land by the sea shall become pastures,
caves for shepherds, and pens for sheep.{e}

“I have listened to Moab’s insults
and the abuse of the Ammonites,
who have mocked my people
and boasted over their borders.

Therefore, as surely as I live,” announces Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel,{f}
“Moab will end up like Sodom,
and Ammon like Gomorrah,
overgrown with weeds, pits of salt,
and permanent ruin.
The rest of my people will loot them;
those of my nation who are left will take their land.”

This is what they get for their arrogance,
for scorning and boasting
against the people of Yahweh of Armies.

Yahweh will terrify them,
for he will wither all the earth’s gods;{g}
and every distant shore of the nations
will worship him, each in its own place.

You also, O Cushites,{h}
shall be slain by my sword.

And he will stretch out his hand against the north
and destroy Assyria,
and he will make Nineveh a desolation,
dry as the wilderness.

Flocks will bed down in her center,
every kind of creature;{i}
the desert owl and the porcupine
will roost on her capitals;
hooting will sound from the windows,
rubble will fill the doorways,
because he has stripped her cedar paneling bare.

This is the exultant city
that dwelt securely,
that said in her heart,
“I am, and there is none else.”
How she has become a desolation,
a lair for wild beasts!
Everyone who passes by her
hisses and shakes his fist.

notes.text: The Hebrew of verses 1–2 is difficult. The verb in verse 1 may mean “gather like stubble,” and the phrase translated “before the decree takes effect” is literally “before the decree gives birth.”
“Hidden” (Hebrew sathar) may echo the name Zephaniah (“Yahweh has hidden”), though the verb is different.
The verse plays on the Hebrew names: Gaza (‘Azzah) will be forsaken (‘azuvah), and Ekron (‘Eqron) will be uprooted (te‘aqer).
The Cherethites were a people of the coast, closely linked with the Philistines and probably from Crete (Kaphtor).
The Hebrew word translated “meadows” (keroth) is uncertain. It may refer to wells or to shepherds’ huts, and it may echo “Cherethites” in verse 5.

Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot, traditionally “the LORD of hosts.” The “armies” are the forces of heaven (the angels and the stars) and sometimes the armies of Israel. The title is translated “Yahweh of Armies” throughout.
Or “he will make lean,” that is, cut off the offerings by which the gods were thought to be fed.
Cush is the upper Nile region (ancient Nubia). Egypt was ruled by a Cushite dynasty until 656 BC.

“Nation” may refer to any kind of creature (“every kind of beast”). The birds and animals named in this verse cannot be identified with certainty. The Septuagint differs in several places, for example “ravens in her porches.”

verses.text:
Woe to her who is rebellious and defiled,
the oppressing city!{a}

I said, ‘Surely you will fear me;
you will accept correction.’
Then her dwelling would not be cut off,
for all that I appointed against her.
But they rose early and made all their deeds corrupt.

“Therefore wait for me,” declares Yahweh,
“until the day that I rise up for the prey.{b}
For my judgment is to gather the nations,
that I may assemble the kingdoms,
to pour my indignation on them,
even all my fierce anger;
for all the earth shall be devoured
by the fire of my zeal.

In that day you will not be ashamed
for any of your doings
in which you transgressed against me;
for then I will take away from among you
those who exult in their pride,
and you shall no longer be haughty
on my holy mountain.

Instead I will leave among you
a poor and humble people,
who will find shelter in Yahweh’s name.

Shout for joy, daughter of Zion;
sing out, Israel!
Rejoice and celebrate with your whole heart,
daughter of Jerusalem!

Behold, at that time I will deal with all who afflict you,
and I will rescue the limping
and gather those who were driven away,
and I will make them a praise and a name
in every land where they were put to shame.{h}

At that time I will lead you home,
and at that time I will assemble you;
I will make you famous and honored
among every people on earth,
when I reverse your misfortunes before your very eyes,” says Yahweh.

notes.text: Hebrew mor’ah, “rebellious,” may play on mar’ah, “seen,” or on Moriah, the temple mount. The city is Jerusalem.
Hebrew la‘ad, “for the prey.” The Septuagint has “for a witness,” reading the same letters as le‘ed.
Literally “I will turn to the peoples a pure lip.” The Wadi Murabba‘at Minor Prophets scroll reads “upon the peoples.”
That is, “side by side, with one accord.”
The Hebrew of the second line is difficult. Some take “the daughter of Putsai” as a place name. The Septuagint has “I will receive my dispersed ones; they shall offer sacrifices to me.”
Literally “he will be silent in his love,” perhaps meaning that he will no longer speak of their sins. The Septuagint has “and shall renew you in his love,” reading yehaddesh for yaharish.
The Hebrew of this verse is obscure, and the translation is uncertain. The Septuagint has “And I will gather your afflicted ones. Alas! who has taken up a reproach against her?”
Literally “in all the earth, their shame.”
